planting.note: Mount divided rhizome sections onto a slab, basket, or tree fern fiber in spring, or pot loosely into a chunky bark-based epiphyte mix, and keep warm and humid while new fronds establish.

directions: This Australian and New Guinea epiphyte produces two distinct kinds of fronds: flat, rounded, papery nest fronds that clasp the host and collect leaf litter and moisture, and tall, deeply dissected fertile fronds that arch outward and give the plant its lush, fountain-like silhouette. Mount it on a slab, hanging basket, or the crook of a tree where its creeping rhizome can climb and branch, and let the nest fronds build up their own humus pocket rather than clearing away the dead material they trap. Give it bright, filtered light and high humidity, watering the root mass thoroughly and letting it approach dryness between soakings since the thick rhizome stores moisture. It tolerates brief dry spells better than many epiphytic ferns, making it a forgiving choice for a shaded porch or greenhouse basket.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide creeping rhizome sections in spring and attach or wedge them onto waterlogged wood, rock, or saturated substrate along a shaded stream-edge or paludarium feature; this species wants its roots permanently wet, not merely moist.

directions: Native to tropical Asian streambanks, this fern gets its common name from the irregular, forked, horn-like lobing of its leathery fronds, a distinctive silhouette unlike the more uniform pinnate fronds of most ferns. It grows naturally rooted at the water's edge or directly submerged on rocks and driftwood in slow-moving streams, making it a favorite for paludariums, bog gardens, and shaded water-feature margins rather than ordinary potting mix. Keep the rhizome constantly wet to fully submerged and provide deep, consistent shade, since both drying out and strong light quickly damage the fronds. New plantlets form readily along the creeping rhizome and can be separated and reattached to fresh substrate once they have their own small root system.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into rich, humusy, well-drained soil in deep shade, mimicking the leaf-littered floor of a tropical hardwood hammock.

directions: Found in South Florida hammocks and throughout the Caribbean, this terrestrial fern bears broad, triangular, finely divided fronds that give it a soft, lacy texture distinct from the coarser strap- and sword-type ferns common in the same habitat. It thrives in the deep, dappled shade and leaf-litter-rich soil of a hardwood hammock understory, and does best in a garden setting with similarly rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil protected from direct sun and drying wind. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form a loose colony rather than aggressively carpeting an area, making it a well-behaved choice for a shaded native-plant woodland bed. Protect it from frost, as it has little cold tolerance outside its subtropical native range.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide the creeping rhizome in spring and mount sections on wood or wedge into a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix in a closed terrarium or vivarium where humidity stays consistently high.

directions: Native to the limestone karst forests of Thailand, this small epiphytic or lithophytic fern is prized for its narrow, undivided fronds that shimmer with an iridescent steel-blue sheen in low light, a structural rather than pigment-based coloration unusual among ferns. It demands very high, constant humidity and struggles in open room air, which has made it a specialty plant for closed terrariums and vivariums rather than conventional houseplant growing. Mount the rhizome on wood, cork, or rock with a thin layer of sphagnum moss rather than burying it, since the roots are adapted to clinging on a surface rather than rooting deep in soil. Keep light bright but indirect, since both deep shade and direct sun cause the blue iridescence to fade.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide creeping, fuzzy rhizome sections in spring and lay them across the surface of a well-drained epiphyte mix or mount on a slab, pinning lightly until new roots anchor it in place.

directions: A close relative of the more widely grown Humata tyermanii bear's-paw fern, this East Asian epiphyte is distinguished by the finer, more deeply toothed cutting of its small triangular fronds, which rise from a creeping, silvery-furred rhizome reminiscent of a small animal's foot. Grow it mounted on a slab or trailing over the rim of a shallow pot filled with a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix, allowing the rhizome to creep over the surface rather than burying it, since covered rhizomes rot readily. It prefers bright, indirect light and steady humidity but tolerates brief dry spells better than many soft-leaved ferns thanks to the moisture-storing rhizome. Protect it from hard frost, though it tolerates cooler nights better than most tropical epiphytic ferns.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide rhizome mats in spring and tuck sections into crevices of a shaded rock garden wall, tufa, or well-drained woodland bed; this species roots naturally on rock faces and old tree bark in its native range.

directions: Unusually cold-hardy for a strap fern, this East Asian species grows naturally as a lithophyte on mossy rocks and as an epiphyte on old tree trunks in Japanese and Chinese forests, forming a dense, low mat of narrow, simple, undivided fronds from a creeping rhizome. It is well suited to a shaded rock garden crevice, tufa wall, or the base of a mossy stump, where it tolerates both drier rock-face conditions and more typical woodland soil moisture. Give it dappled shade and good drainage, since standing water around the rhizome causes rot even though the plant otherwise tolerates considerable dryness between waterings. Established mats need very little care beyond an occasional top-dressing of leaf mold and are slow enough growing that division is rarely needed more than once every several years.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
